synopsis: South Africa is the booklet’s main case of mandatory collision-prevention intervention preceding validation standards: its TMM regulations were promulgated on 27 February 2015, and the critical sub-regulations commenced on 21 December 2022 with no transitional period [f11458, f11461, f15555]. The requirements call for diesel-powered machines to detect and warn, slow to a safe speed and automatically brake if no action prevents a potential collision, and fail to safe without human intervention [f15556, f11456]. Although one chapter describes a mandate for all surface and underground TMMs, the detailed legal account specifies diesel-powered machines and stipulated significant collision risks; coverage of battery-electric machines remains unclear [f1087, f2279, f2280, f15559]. Industry developed surface-TMM verification specifications in 2025 and 2026, including one dated 29 August 2025; MOSH requires verification of each type, model and serial number where braking characteristics differ, while mine-specific codes of practice and commissioning add another acceptance layer [f11459, f555, f5613, f2283]. Safe intervention itself needs validation: MOSH warns of unintended consequences from unsafe slowing or stopping, and fixed stopping gaps can obstruct loading unless the collision-prevention system is switched off [f5815, f3344]. South Africa recorded nine TMM-related deaths in 2024 versus six in 2023, but published scenarios do not establish how many automatic braking could have prevented; the reported single TMM collision death in 2022 is unverified and cannot be directly compared with the broader transport-and-mining fatality total [f3140, f3141, f3145, f3144].
